passage: English period note, Rajni. We did riddles today. I asked, "What has hands but can't clap?" Kashish, nine, said, "A clock!" and then added, "And a pair of gloves on a washing line." Later a boy called her "Kashish the Quiz Machine," and she stiffened for a second. Then she saw him grinning, not smirking, and she did a robot voice: "Processing... correct." The class laughed with her. Last term she used to cry at nicknames. Next Friday I will hold a pun hour and talk about teasing that includes versus teasing that hurts.

qa.q: Which riddle did Rajni ask?
qa.a: "What has hands but can't clap?"

qa.q: Why did Kashish decide the nickname was friendly?
qa.a: She felt wary at first and stiffened, but then saw the boy grinning, not smirking, and read it as fun rather than meanness.

qa.q: Why is Rajni's plan to discuss different kinds of teasing useful?
qa.a: It helps children notice cues like a grin or a smirk and learn when teasing is friendly and when it hurts.

qa.q: How might the boy feel when Kashish does the robot voice?
qa.a: Relieved and pleased that she took his nickname as a joke and played along.

grounding: It shows a girl solving riddle logic and reading a nickname as friendly teasing rather than malice.

passage:
Diary, Wednesday.
Gautam Bhaiya looked at my science model and said, "Wow, Deepika, a leaning tower. Very modern." I got angry and said he's mean. Then he laughed and said, "It's a joke! It's nice. Just fix the left leg." I looked again. My volcano stand was leaning a lot. I was still a bit cross, but I laughed too. Later at dinner Papa said, "Oh great, more karela," and Bhaiya winked at me, and I got it straight away: Papa hates karela! I think I understand Bhaiya's jokes better now. Mostly.

qa.q: Which part of the model did Gautam say to fix?
qa.a: The left leg.

qa.q: Why did Deepika get angry at first?
qa.a: Deepika took his "leaning tower" comment as a mean insult before realising it was a joke with a real tip inside.

qa.q: What could Deepika do next time it's unclear whether a comment is a joke?
qa.a: Look at the person's face and ask, "Are you joking?" before getting upset.

qa.q: How might Gautam see his own teasing?
qa.a: He probably meant it as affectionate fun with a helpful hint, not to hurt Deepika.

grounding: It shows a child learning to read an older brother's sarcasm and teasing as playful rather than mean.

passage: At the Tuesday haat in their village, Jagdish Kaka, who sold peanuts, liked to test the children. "Urmila, what goes up but never comes down?" Urmila, ten, frowned at the sky. "A kite? No, that comes down." "Think." She grinned. "Your age, Kaka!" He clapped. Then he said, "Your brain is so sharp, I'll use it to cut my onions." For a moment Urmila wasn't sure. Then she saw his eyes crinkle and laughed. "So I get free peanuts for sharpening?" He poured an extra handful into her paper cone.

qa.q: What did Jagdish Kaka sell?
qa.a: He sold peanuts.

qa.q: Why was Urmila unsure for a moment after the onion comment?
qa.a: She had to decide whether it was a compliment or an odd jab, until his crinkled eyes showed it was friendly.

qa.q: What did Urmila's reply show about handling teasing?
qa.a: Answering with her own joke kept things light and playful instead of taking offence.

qa.q: How might Jagdish Kaka feel when Urmila jokes back?
qa.a: Delighted, which is why he gives her an extra handful of peanuts. 😊

grounding: It shows a girl solving riddle logic and recognising an elder's playful teasing as affection.

passage: In a Toronto school lunchroom, Kwame held up his sandwich. 'Why did the bread go to school?' Esther groaned. 'Because it wanted to be well-bread?' Kwame laughed, 'You always get it!' Later, when Esther spilled her juice, Kwame said, 'Great job, Miss Graceful.' Esther paused, then saw his grin and laughed. 'Thanks, Mr. Helpful,' she said, handing him a napkin. She knew he wasn't being mean; he always teased her when he liked her company.

qa.q: What was Kwame's riddle about?
qa.a: It was about bread going to school.

qa.q: How did Esther feel when Kwame called her 'Miss Graceful'?
qa.a: She paused, unsure at first, then felt amused when she saw his grin, knowing he always teased her when he liked her company.

qa.q: What skill helps Esther handle teasing like this?
qa.a: She checks his face and their history before reacting, which helps her tell playful teasing from real unkindness.

qa.q: What would change if a stranger had called Esther 'Miss Graceful'?
qa.a: She might take it as mean, since she would not have the friendship and cues to read it as playful.

grounding: Illustrates a child understanding puns and light teasing without taking them as malice, set in Canada.

passage: In Class 5, the teacher held a riddle contest. 'What has keys but can't open locks?' Devika's hand shot up. 'A piano!' Omkar muttered, 'Oh, look, our genius.' Devika turned around sharply, then saw him smiling and giving a thumbs up. She grinned and whispered, 'Jealous?' He laughed. Next riddle, Omkar got it right. Devika clapped and said, 'Look who's awake today!' They both burst out laughing, and the teacher shook her head, smiling.

qa.q: What was Devika's answer to the riddle?
qa.a: She said, 'A piano!'

qa.q: What did Devika realise when she saw Omkar's thumbs up?
qa.a: She realised his 'genius' comment was playful teasing, not an insult, so she relaxed and joked back.

qa.q: How could a teacher help students understand teasing like this?
qa.a: She could talk about how tone, smiles and friendship help us tell playful teasing from hurtful comments.

qa.q: How might the teacher see their joking?
qa.a: She seems amused and not worried, seeing it as friendly banter. 🙂

grounding: Shows children understanding riddles and sarcastic teasing as friendly rather than malicious, in a classroom.
